title: How Fair Trade Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain fair trade: its origins in 1950s alternative trade organizations and the Dutch labeling group Solidaridad, how the Fairtrade Labeling Organization (FLO) licenses and certifies supply chains, the core tenets (middlemen contracts, direct trade, co-op structures, social premium, minimum prices), the income disparity between chocolate consumers and cocoa producers, and criticisms such as market distortion and co-op corruption. The episode also covers misleading "fairly treated" or "naturally" labeling, includes a sponsorship appeal for Cooperative for Education (co-ed) in Guatemala, and closes with a listener mail about grief and a request for an episode on pineapples.
topics: supply and demand criticism of fair trade

entities.name: Is the free market really free?

segments.title: Opening banter and water myth
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about episode count, drinking water, and Josh's back pain, then introduce the idea that producers should earn a livable wage.

segments.title: Free market versus fair pay
segments.summary: They frame fair trade as a response to a free market in which power has concentrated among a few international players, and say it is not a call for communism.

segments.title: Fair trade labels versus misleading claims
segments.summary: They distinguish certified fair trade labels from vague marketing claims like 'fairly treated' or 'naturally good', and compare this to organic certification.

segments.title: History: alternative trade and Solidaridad
segments.summary: Fair trade began in the 1950s with alternative trade organizations seeking to cut out middlemen. Solidaridad, a Dutch group, created the labeling. A 2001 coffee price example shows farmers got 45 cents per pound while fair trade buyers paid $1.21, and fair trade sets minimum prices.

segments.title: How certification works
segments.summary: A roaster licenses fair trade coffee from the FLO or another labeling body. Inspectors visit farms, check practices and sustainability, and conduct periodic follow-ups. Supply chains require contracts of at least six months.

segments.title: Core tenets and criticisms
segments.summary: Key principles are contracts with middlemen, direct trade, co-op formation, national labor law compliance, social premium funds for community projects, and minimum prices based on cost surveys. Criticisms include market distortion, oversupply, and corruption in co-ops.

segments.title: Global income disparity
segments.summary: The hosts compare annual incomes in 2005 for farmers in Ethiopia, Malawi, Somalia, Congo, Eritrea and similar countries with average US daily spending, and argue fair trade is not welfare.

segments.title: Growth and marketing of fair trade
segments.summary: About 800,000 farmers benefit worldwide, with growth in fair trade coffee. The hosts suggest broader marketing and product diversification.

segments.title: Cooperative for Education sponsorship appeal
segments.summary: Hosts promote Cooperative for Education, which supports 54 Mayan middle school students in Guatemala with scholarships, seeking sponsors at $70 or $35 a month.

segments.title: Listener mail on grief and pineapples
segments.summary: A listener named John writes about the death of his brother Mike and says the grief podcast helped. He asks for an episode on pineapples. The hosts close with social media and website info.
